title: Pacing housework with arthritis: cleaning, laundry and chores without the payback (UK guide)

content:
Housework is easier on painful joints when you stop trying to do it all in one go. Split big jobs into short pieces with rests in between, do the heaviest jobs at your best time of day, sit down for anything you can, and use lighter, long-handled or electric tools so your hands, back, hips and knees do less. Plan a whole week rather than a single day, so a busy day with visitors is followed by an easier one. If chores still leave you exhausted or in more pain, ask your GP about an occupational therapist, or your council for a needs assessment. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself to get through a busy day.

This guide is for people with arthritis who find cleaning, laundry, cooking and tidying leave them sore or wiped out, and for the family who want to help. For the general method behind it, see how to pace activities properly. For ways to move and grip that put less strain on your joints, see joint protection for everyday tasks.

Why housework causes so much payback

Many people with arthritis know the pattern: a good morning, so you clean the whole kitchen, change the beds and do two loads of washing, then spend the next day or two in more pain and too tired to do much at all. This is sometimes called boom and bust. Chores are hard on joints because they mix things arthritis dislikes:

  • bending and reaching, such as making beds, loading the washing machine or cleaning the bath
  • gripping and twisting, such as wringing cloths, opening bottles or holding a vacuum cleaner
  • carrying, such as laundry baskets, shopping and buckets of water
  • standing still for a long time, such as ironing or washing up
  • doing the same movement over and over without a break

The aim of pacing is not to do less forever. It is to spread the load so you can keep doing the things that matter to you, more evenly, without paying for it afterwards. NHS advice on living with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis includes staying active, getting help with daily tasks and finding easier ways to do things.

The three Ps: plan, prioritise, pace

Occupational therapists often describe pacing with three Ps.

  • Plan. Look at the week, not just today. Write down the jobs that need doing and spread them out, so no single day is full of heavy tasks.
  • Prioritise. Ask what really needs doing, what can wait, what someone else could do and what could be done less often. A tidy-enough home is fine.
  • Pace. Break each job into short pieces and stop for a rest before the pain or tiredness builds, not after. One room, then a sit down, then the next.

A simple test is to work out how long you can do a task on a bad day without it flaring your pain, and use that as your starting chunk on every day. On good days, resist the urge to catch up on everything. An activity diary for a week or two can show which jobs cost you most and when your best time of day is.

Easier ways to do common chores

Small changes to how you do a job often help more than pushing through.

Cleaning

  • Use a lightweight cordless vacuum cleaner or a robot vacuum instead of a heavy upright, and do one room at a time.
  • Use long-handled dusters, mops with wringers you work with your foot or a lever, and spray bottles with large triggers.
  • Keep a set of cleaning things upstairs and downstairs so you are not carrying them on the stairs.
  • Clean the bath or shower while sitting on a stool or the side of the bath, or straight after a shower while you are already there and warm.

Laundry and ironing

  • Wash smaller loads more often so the basket is lighter, and use a basket on wheels or a trolley.
  • Raise the washing machine or put the basket on a chair so you are not bending to the floor.
  • Use a drying rack at waist height, or a tumble dryer if you have one, rather than reaching up to a washing line.
  • Iron sitting down on a perching stool, iron less (many clothes do not need it) and choose clothes that do not crease easily.

Beds

  • Use a fitted bottom sheet and a duvet rather than sheets and blankets you have to tuck in.
  • Change the bed in stages, such as the pillowcases one day and the duvet cover the next, or ask for help with the duvet cover.

Kitchen and shopping

  • Sit to prepare food and wash up where you can, and keep the things you use most between hip and shoulder height.
  • Use a kettle tipper, jar opener, lightweight pans and a trolley to move things around. Our guide to kitchen adaptations has more ideas.
  • Shop online for heavy things, or shop little and often with a wheeled shopping trolley.

The NHS has a page on household gadgets and equipment to make life easier, and Living Made Easy lists independent information on equipment. See our guide to choosing arthritis-friendly products before you buy.

Visitors, family days and weekends

Busy days are often the ones you look forward to most, such as grandchildren visiting, a family meal or a day out. They are also the ones most likely to cause a flare if you get the house ready, cook, host and tidy up all in one go.

  • Spread the preparation over the days before, and leave an easy day afterwards with nothing heavy planned.
  • Ask visitors to bring food, make the drinks or help clear up. Most people are glad to be asked.
  • Keep visits to a length that suits you, and plan a sit-down in a comfortable chair rather than being on your feet the whole time.
  • For a weekend away or a big event, plan rest breaks into the day and pack the day before.

Keep moving, not just resting

Pacing is not the same as stopping. NICE guidance for osteoarthritis says exercise and staying active are a core part of treatment. Light chores can count as movement, and resting all the time can make joints stiffer and muscles weaker, which makes housework harder in the long run. Build in short spells of gentle exercise as well, such as the ideas in our exercise for beginners guide. If tiredness is the main problem rather than pain, see arthritis fatigue explained.

When to get help with housework

If you have paced and adapted and chores still leave you in pain or exhausted, or you have stopped doing things that keep you safe and well, it is time to ask for help.

  • Occupational therapy. An occupational therapist (OT) can look at how you do tasks at home and suggest equipment and easier methods. Ask your GP, or see our guide to occupational therapy for arthritis. If you are on a waiting list, see what to do while you wait for community OT.
  • A council needs assessment. Anyone can ask their council for a free needs assessment. Describe your bad days, including jobs that cause significant pain or take you much longer.
  • Benefits. If arthritis affects your daily living, you may be able to claim Attendance Allowance if you are over State Pension age, or PIP if you are under it. Some people use this money towards a cleaner or help with shopping. See our benefits and PIP guide.
  • Family and friends. Agree which jobs others will do regularly, rather than waiting until you cannot manage.

When it is more than tiredness

Contact your GP if pain or tiredness is getting steadily worse, if joints are newly swollen, or if you feel unwell, are losing weight or are very short of breath doing things you managed before. If you have inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, contact your rheumatology helpline if you think you are having a flare.

  • For urgent advice, use NHS 111 online or call NHS 111.
  • Call 999 or go to A&E if you have a fall and cannot get up, have chest pain, or have a hot, swollen, very painful joint and feel feverish or unwell.

For carers and family

  • Offer to take on the heaviest jobs, such as changing the bed or carrying the laundry, rather than everything. Doing everything can make the person less active.
  • Help set up the home so things are easier to reach and carry.
  • If you are doing a lot of caring, ask your council for a carer's assessment.

Common questions

How long should I do housework before I rest?

There is no set time. Start with what you can manage on a bad day without increasing your pain, rest before you need to, and build up slowly over the weeks.

Is it lazy to leave the housework?

No. Choosing which jobs matter, and leaving the rest, is part of managing a long-term condition well.

Can I get free equipment for housework?

Some equipment is available free from the council or NHS after an assessment. Ask about an occupational therapy or needs assessment before you buy.
